April 15, 1986
Employment Equity
The House resumed consideration of Bill C-62, an Act respecting employment equity, as reported (with amendments) from a legislative committee; and Motion No. 21A (Mr. Allmand).
When the House broke at 1 p.m. the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) had the floor. Resuming debate.

Mr. Speaker, what we are debating is an amendment put forward by the Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East (Mr. Allmand) which would make public the action plans of employers. When the Minister introduced the legislation she did not introduce any measures with respect to action plans at all. After a great many groups appeared before the committee the Minister introduced an amendment to the Bill to provide for action plans. However, these action plans are not to be made public. What is the purpose of having an action plan if it is not to be made public?
What we are calling on the Government to do is accept this particular amendment in order to make the action plan available to the workers in a plant or in industries which are affected by the Bill. We are also calling on the Government to make the action plans public to the Human Rights Commission. Gordon Fairweather, the Chairman of the Human Rights Commission, has said that he would like to have access to these particular action plans. Under this legislation they will not be made available. I call upon the House to listen to Mr. Fair-weather. He is a distinguished Canadian, a distinguished former parliamentarian and a member of the Conservative Party. He is a very progressive member of that Party. I think we should accede to his wishes.
I wish to refer the House once again to the speech made by Gordon Fairweather in which he stated that the action plans of employees under this Bill should be made available to the Human Rights Commission. They should be made public. I agree with Mr. Fairweather's words. I agree with Motion No. 21 A. I think it is a reasonable amendment to the Bill which has been introduced by a member of the Liberal Party. It is supported by ourselves. I think all reasonable members of the Conservative Party would have to support it as well. After all, the Conservative Party is the Party which campaigned for freedom of information. Why not support this motion to ensure these action plans are made public?
[ Translation]

Mr. Speaker, I should like to draw the attention of the House to the amendment to Clause 5 of the Act respecting employment equity. It concerns the plan of goals to be prepared by the companies
involved and the implementation of such plans to achieve a more equitable situation for the designated groups, the minority groups in our society, and people whose future is not very promising unless we take concrete measures.
Here is the amendment, and I quote Clause 5:
5. (1) An employer shall, in respect of each year, prepare a plan setting out (a) the goals that he employer intends to achieve in implementing employment equity in the year or years to which the plan relates; and (b) the timetable for the implementation of those goals.
And second, the reference to the retention of the plan.
(2) A copy of a plan prepared under subsection (1) shall be retained by employer at the employer's principal place of business in Canada for a period of at least three years after the last year in respect of which the plan is prepared.
Mr. Speaker, I find fascinating the suggestion that the plan be kept in a drawer or at the work place. But if we want real improvement, if we want the legislation to have more impact, if we expect more than pious wishes, if we do not want this to be a joke or the kind of academic exercise a la Harvard Business School, if instead we want it to become an open plan of action so that all people concerned will know what this is all about, then I think the amendments proposed by my colleague are very important. These amendments indicate what the employer must do. A copy of a plan prepared under subsection (I) shall be:
(b)	communicated to the employer's employees and any existing bargaining agent; and
(c)	made available to the Human Rights Commission, on request.
In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, at least that makes sense. Why go through that exercise if nobody is to know what it is all about? Why go through the motions if nothing comes out of it, if everything is done in great secrecy?
I simply fail to see why, at least during the three years after the last year of a plan, a plan should be prepared if nobody is going to see it. If it is to remain in a file or a safety vault, why waste the time of the major employers? In my judgment, it does not make sense at all.

The Bill, which did not originally promote action plans with targets and timetables, has been amended, at least in that sense. It is a substantive amendment. It is an amendment which only makes good sense. What on earth good is there in developing a plan to sit around a table in order to take a look at information from Statistics Canada and then file that information away in a drawer? No one will ever see it. For the life of me 1 cannot understand why the Government would not find this a logical follow-up on what seems to be the first of the two objectives under the plans in terms of goals to be prepared. It is the type of action which should follow on the heels of working on those plans.
Not only do plans need to be prepared, they must also be made available to the employees-the people involved in this whole process-and to the Human Rights Commission upon request. Unless employees and the target groups about which we are talking are aware of the new opportunities, then they
April 15, 1986

are unlikely to apply. It is as if the Government has looked only at voluntary measures. If this law is not applied to the principle of submitting these plans for revision, then there is no point in having them. If the Human Rights Commission cannot access employers' plans then it will be unable to assess whether the measures planned by the employer are adequate and, indeed, whether the plans have been implemented.
The other part of the farce is that if the plans are not implemented, then nothing happens. All one has to say is that the plans have been drawn up. If they do not have a set of plans, they can be fined, but who knows what they have if the plans are filed away in drawers? At least the plans should have to be submitted somewhere so someone knows they exist. They should be sent to the Employment and Immigration offices so that it may be determined if they are really targeting the population and they need to be viewed in light of the statistics which are being undertaken at this point.
We had to fight hard enough to get StatsCanada to continue so that we will know where we are at and can take a good look at the composition of our society. What is the point of doing that if we are not going to apply the findings? I think this amendment is only an intelligent progression that would enable the law to be applied in its entirety.
I would like to suggest that not only should the plans be retained by the employer at the employer's principal place of residence in Canada for a period of three years, but as well that they be communicated to the employees and any existing bargaining agent, and further that they be made available to the Human Rights Commission on request. I would like very much to support my colleague's amendment in this regard.
There is no doubt that both the Advisory Council on the Status of Women and the Human Rights Commissioner, Mr. Gordon Fairweather, feel equally strongly that this amendment is a necessity if we want to measure progress in society in any way. I have said from the very beginning that the concept of this Bill could be very effective for the target groups, but there is no way that it will be effective if we continue with the farce of keeping secret the plans of action that one has undertaken.
1 would ask the Parliamentary Secretary if he and the Minister have agreed to these amendments which make sound sense and would give the Bill some coherence and potential for action. I sincerely hope that they will take this into consideration and that the Government will support this amendment.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to bring one or two comments about this amendment to the Parliamentary Secretary and through him to the Minister. The game the Government intends to play is called: "I've got a secret". I must say that I am extremely disturbed over the Government's reluctance to allow any voluntary enforcement of goals and targets set by an employer, because these goals and targets will not in fact be communicated to employees
Employment Equity
except in the better workplaces where the employer tries to be open about this process. The exact areas where employment equity is most needed are those areas in which there will be the least amount of information made available.
Suppose there was a law in this country indicating that we would wipe out discrimination against a particular religious group, but this was going to be done in stages. We would tell employers that they have to set goals for eliminating discrimination against that particular religious group but they are not to communicate those goals to the people who are affected- why I do not know. When we put it that way it sounds pretty awful, and the reason it sounds pretty awful is that it is pretty awful.
I would have thought that the Parliamentary Secretary, being himself a member of a group which has suffered a great deal of discrimination in the past, would have been sensitive to this issue and would, if he has not been given the authority to do so by his Minister, say that he himself personally endorses the change even though the Government is not prepared to go along with it. That is the kind of courage we would like to see displayed by that Parliamentary Secretary. We do not want to see him go along with something which will make useless this particular provision in the Bill.
Clause 5 of the Bill, which was inserted in response to a great deal of pressure during the course of the hearings, requires that an employer shall prepare a plan each year to set out the goals the employer intends to achieve in implementing employment equity as well as a timetable for implementing those goals. That would be a step forward, except that both the amendment put by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom), and the amendment which we are debating, put by the Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East (Mr. Allmand), relate to the salient point that there has to be a way by which the people affected have cognizance of what those goals and targets for implementation actually are. That is not the case in the Bill as it now stands.
The proposed amendments would simply ensure that in one way or other the information be communicated to employees. If there is a bargaining agent, the information should go to the bargaining agent. It can go to the employees by means of a company memorandum or by being posted on bulletin boards throughout the workplace and copies could be made available to those employees who are interested in receiving copies. There are different ways of making information available, and the Parliamentary Secretary knows very well that there are well established ways of communicating this kind of information in the workplace.
I draw to the attention of the Parliamentary Secretary the high-flying language of Clause 2, the purpose of the Bill, which indicates that the purpose is to correct the conditions of disadvantage in employment experienced by women and the other groups affected, by giving effect to the principle that employment equity means more than treating persons in the

April 15, 1986
Employment Equity
same way, but also requires special measures and the accommodation of differences. How the devil do people know how that is seen by the employer if in fact the employer does not have to communicate just what it is he intends to do?
Clause 4 of the Bill indicates that the employer is required to implement employment equity in consultation with designated representatives of the employees, however those designated representatives happen to be chosen. If I consult with the Government, but then at the end of the day the Government says it is not going to tell me what the goals and targets are, then 1 will have no means of knowing what is going on and that is a pretty weak consultation. In fact, that takes the meat out of the process. That is not consultation.
The Canadian Human Rights Commission is a small body. It cannot monitor the actions of every employer who falls under federal regulation. There has to be a certain amount of voluntary enforcement. In fact, that is the system on which a great deal of federal law is based. Standards are set out and means are provided by which people can make complaints if they feel that the standards are not being respected. However, such a process is impossible if people are not allowed to know to what extent the employer's achievements, if any, reach the plan which the employer worked out, presumably in consultation with the employees. Only if the employer chooses to share that information will that be able to occur.
Under the Human Rights Act, the Human Rights Commission has the power to look at the implementation of employment equity, but there again the amendment would give the Human Rights Commission access on demand to the employer's plans and targets. However, because that is not as yet required, another obstacle is put before the Human Rights Commission. Conceivably it will have to go to the courts in order to get the information which in fact should be made freely available.
Canada Employment Centres are meant to ensure contract compliance in the case of larger employers who do business with the federal Government, but there again one of the ways of ensuring compliance is to see how targets and goals are being met. But that information is not going to be made available to employees. There is no requirement that it be made available to the Canada Employment Centres either. The information could simply be locked in a safe, and if anyone came to try to find out about the plans the employer need simply indicate that he has kept the information in a safe for three years where it has been safe from any form of public scrutiny.

Mr. Speaker, I want to stress the fact that Clause 5 of the Bill as drafted after committee consideration is so weak that it is practically useless.
It is useless because the employer must spell out in a plan each one of his goals with respect to employment equity, but this plan would not be unveiled to the employees, the unions
representing the employees, the Canadian Human Rights Commission, or the manpower centres.
So nobody will know the goals of the employer because the Government refuses to give that right to the employees. Mr. Speaker, I am wondering just how they can have the kind of consultation referred to in the subclauses of the Bill when the people who will be consulted will have no idea whether the employer has accepted or rejected their suggestions. They might even be given contradictory information. The employer will tell them: Yes, I agree, it is a good idea, your suggestions are excellent. But the day after, the employer prepares a plan of goals which completely ignores the remarks and suggestions made by the employees. But ask the employer whether he considers suggestions made by his employees and the employer will answer: of course. I promised I would consider their suggestions. That is, he considers them and then ignores them, and his employees will never know whether he included a substantial portion of their suggestions in the action plan set up by the employer for a three-year period.
As I said earlier, I am amazed, especially since the Parliamentary Secretary belongs to a group that has suffered terrible discrimination in the past, that he should fail to see how important it is to shine the light of information on all this so there are no secrets and employers, employees and unions discuss the plans together. That is what they want, Mr. Speaker. But in our society, we often get no further than voluntary compliance with legislation passed by the Parliament of Canada. In this case, Mr. Speaker, it would be impossible for people to try and influence the employer and make him meet the objectives set in his action plan, because his employees do not know what they are, except when the employer is a good employer who is serious about meeting his obligations.

speechtext: There is a purpose in listening. There is a purpose in communicating. There is a purpose in putting into effect a piece of legislation which will work. Philosophically we do not agree, but we on all sides of the House want to ensure that there is true equality. We want to ensure that we are not patronizing and that we have results.
What does that have to do with publishing a plan?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
speechtext: Employers are required to consult with their employees. There is no need to mention the word "brief since the Bill already specifies that it will be three years. Employers will be encouraged in guidelines to make the plans available to employees.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
speechtext:
The guidelines to employers will specify that a good employment strategy includes making the plans available to employees. The plans will not be available to the Canadian Human Rights Commission on request. However, the Canadian Human Rights Commission will have access to the plans when investigating complaints.
Gordon Fairweather, Commissioner of the Canadian Human Rights Commission, indicated during the committee hearings that the reported data would be sufficient to initiate complaints under the Canadian Human Rights Act. The Commission can initiate complaints, examine data and plans and, if necessary, appoint tribunals which have the authority to impose sanctions where findings of discrimination are made.
What about freedom of information? Didn't you used to stand for that?

speechtext: Since Members are so wonderful in quoting Mr. Fairweather, a great Canadian, a very concerned man and one of the foremost leaders of human rights in the world, I too would like to have a moment to quote him.
You are talking about everybody but the target groups.
Why don't you give him a chance to speak, you nerd?
Is that a parliamentary word?

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, please.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
speechtext:
I should like to refer to what Mr. Gordon Fairweather said at the fifty-fifth annual meeting of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce last September. He said: "I am convinced that the time for affirmative action is now, but let me make it very clear that I do not at this stage advocate mandatory affirmative action".

April 15, 1986
Employment Equity
That is not what is being proposed here.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
speechtext: That is what he stated, that he did not want mandatory affirmative action. Affirmative action does not have to be the same thing as quotas, if we get on with the job and start to show some real progress without them. We want to get on with the job. Let us pass the Bill, let us put employment equity into effect, and five years down the way when we review it together we will all praise the progress we have made.

Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that the Government-in this particular case the Hon. Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Weiner)-is in fact repeating to the House, to the people of Canada and to those groups which want some kind of protection and equality the following old ditty:
"Mother, may I go out to swim?
Yes my darling daughter,
Hang your clothes on the hickory bush,
But don't go near the water."
That is the kind of thinking the Government is asking us to follow. I do not know whether the appropriate word to describe such an approach would be "hypocrisy". However, it certainly is an attempt by the Government to act as if it were doing something, when it knows perfectly well that it is not. It is pretending really to care about a certain group, but it is not going to give them the protection it is pretending it will give them. That underlies the Government's response to this motion.
This motion relates to the need for action plans to be known. We heard the convoluted thinking of the last speaker. He said that the Canadian Human Rights Commission cannot have access to this information, but can request it when it wants to prosecute or act. How can the Canadian Human Rights Commission know whether it wants to act unless it can get the information? That is double-talk. To put it at its nicest, it is a catch-22.
The handicapped who came to the Hill yesterday to protest know this double-talk for what it is. They know that this Bill simply requires companies to make a report with some statistics which they can then hide in their drawers for three years. After kicking, screaming, and resisting, the Conservative Party finally agreed that there should be a plan, but no one can see the plan. It is tragic, or laughable. In any case, it is totally unacceptable to any reasonable, sincere person.
We are not talking only about human rights here. We are talking about human responsibilities. The Government does not seem able to accept human responsibilities. Through the way in which it has handled this equality Bill, it is obvious that the Government does not know what human rights are. It has no idea of how it is necessary for Parliament to be responsible for the protection of the interests of large numbers of citizens.
Women represent at least 51 per cent of our population. One in every eight Canadians, which amounts to millions of our citizens, is disabled. The native people represent a very large section of our community. Visible minority groups also form a very large percentage of our population. A responsible Government would provide legislation to act responsibly in the interests of those people. This Government is not doing so and is fighting, in a most hypocritical way, resolutions which give some meaning to this Bill which, at the present time, is nothing but a bunch of words.
The Government must take the responsibility of ensuring that corporations and companies are responsible to their employees, to the communities which they serve, and to the taxpayers which often support those corporations. We are asking that the taxpayers who fall within these groups be given the right of access to jobs. The Government is not showing responsibility, nor is it calling upon companies to be responsible with regard to the people of the country by making plans to ensure that proper and equal access is provided to all Canadians, and to ensure that their plans are made known so their records can be measured against those plans. That is precisely what this motion is all about.
It is absolutely incredible that the Government is taking evasive tactics by requiring companies to provide action plans, but keeping those plans secret. I call upon the Parliamentary Secretary to re-examine his thinking on this matter and to explain the purpose of having such a plan if the plan is not to be made available to the Canadian Human Rights Commission. Why should a company go to the trouble of making a plan if it stays in the files? It is absurd to require such an exercise. We asked for an action plan because we wanted action. This is inaction.
One cannot conclude other than that the Government is not really sincere about employment equity. It has totally evaded Judge Abella's recommendation to ensure that the Bill has teeth. She said that the passage of a Bill without teeth would be to continue as we have before. We have really made no step forward other than jawboning. I have been speaking to a lot of human rights people. I have been talking to people in the churches concerned with human responsibility. They feel that in terms of this Bill the Government should go back to the drawing board and re-examine its purposes. If the Government passes this bill it will only hinder the cause. The Bill will have practically no effect in terms of bringing about immediate action for the people who have been waiting for the Government to fulfil its promises.
If the Canadian Human Rights Commission wants information, it will have to use sleuths. It will have to guess what companies are doing. It will not have ready access to reports on companies' plans. It can only guess what those plans are, and that means it can do nothing. It will have nothing more than figures with regard to the companies' intentions. We will throw an enormous task upon the back of the Canadian
April 15, 1986

Human Rights Commission which we know it cannot perform. We are handcuffing the commission.
This motion requests that this information be made available to the commission upon request. Why would the Government not be delighted to go along with that part of the resolution? It should not be necessary for the Canadian Human Rights Commission to scramble around to find information when it thinks something is wrong. The Government wants the Canadian Human Rights Commission to play a guessing game and look stupid and ineffective which will give the groups that are discriminated against a sense of frustration and a feeling that the commission is no good. People will say that the commission is incompetent and inept and it will be blamed for that which the Government should be blamed for.

Mr. Speaker, it is difficult to determine whether the rejection of this amendment was due to silliness, stupidity or unconscionable trickery. In response to a significant concern, 1 heard the Parliamentary Secretary telling us that he lived in a good neighbourhood where people worked hard. He told us that his father came here with a nickel. That was his explanation for the denial of this simple amendment. Let me tell him that the women, the disabled and native people of this country reject that. Let me tell him that people like my great, great grandfather who were brought or came to this country as former slaves with less than a nickel in their pockets will not accept that as an explanation.
The fact is that this Government did not in the first instance want to have goals. That is why we have this silly arrangement in this Bill which separates the process from the goals. Having conceded that there should be a definition of goals, year by year, how silly it is to reject having those goals revealed to those directly involved! It has to be a deliberate attempt to sabotage the intent of the clause which adopts the goals. There can be no answer except trickery. I cannot believe that the Government would be so stupid as not to realize that the one way to ensure that an employer will implement serious employment equity processes is by ensuring that every employee subject to those processes and benefiting from those goals knows what the goals are. Could it be possible that the Hon. Member does not know of incident after incident of complaints of discrimination against employers where the excuse has been that the employee responsible for hiring was unaware that the company had a non-discriminatory or affirmative action program?
What concerns me most of all is that this is another example of this Government's refusal to address the needs of those people who are supposed to be benefiting from this legislation. We know the scenario. It is to go slow and not to offend those who are responsible for what many people who are victims regard as a criminal act, that is, the rejection of these people for a job, the denial to them of economic opportunity, the denial of the opportunity to participate in this society in a way
Employment Equity
that would accord them independence. That is what is at issue here.
Does this Government not have the will to address the needs that exist? It cannot be denied now that this Parliamentary Secretary and the Minister he represents are so lacking in conscience that they will pass a shadow of a Bill, one with no substance, and one which will deny the needs of those whose needs this Bill is supposed to meet.
Let us give reconsideration to this denial. Let us examine what is being said. Let us consider the fact that you have at least accepted that there will be goals set year by year. Give us an explanation different from the history of your family, the neighbourhood in which you live, and different from this oft-repeated notion that those who are not visibly definable as minorities have sometimes achieved success in a way which leads them to believe others are not denied that success because of their colour, their sex, their disability, or because they are a member of the aboriginal peoples of this country. Reconsider this and put yourself in the shoes of those who cannot deny to which group they belong and therefore have no support in fighting the discrimination they have experienced in many ways all their lives without the recourse this Bill is supposed to provide, which in fact this Bill manipulates in so many ways so that recourse will not be there at all.

He said: Mr. Speaker, I have presented three amendments here, all of which amend Clause 6 of the Bill, the reporting clause. This clause at present is the only clause which can be considered a sanction. It says that employers who must introduce employment equity must report certain information about their workforce. I presume that the purpose is, as it should be, that once you know what is going on in your workforce, you will be able to tell whether employment equity or affirmative action programs are necessary, whether there has been a lack of progress and so on. My amendments are meant to improve Clause 6, the reporting section. Since these amendments are all grouped together for purposes of debate I will go through them one by one. Amendment 25A is an amendment to sub-clause (d) of Clause 6. At the present time Sub-clause (d) says that the employer must report:
The number of employees hired, promoted and terminated and the degree of representation in those numbers of persons in designated groups.
Mr. Speaker, that is good as far as it goes. You have to report the numbers of native people, visible minorities, women
and disabled people who have been hired, promoted and terminated. My amendment would add to these three categories of those who are hired, promoted and terminated. We would add those who are trained, transferred and demoted.
The reasoning is as follows. If you do not train the women at the bottom of the ladder in your labour force, or the visible minorities, they are not going to get into middle management, they are not going to get to the top. If you are aiming for a situation where you have good representation of these target groups, not only at the bottom of your labour force but in the middle and at the top, we should know who is being trained.
The next amendment concerns those who are transferred. Transfers are used by employers to punish or to reward employees. Those whom they want out of their hair they send to places like-now, 1 have to be careful here. If they want to reward them they certainly send them to Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East and Montreal, in general, and to the Province of Quebec, that is natural. You can be promoted in one month and demoted six months later. Sometimes what appears to be a lateral transfer in the firm ends up, in fact, to be a demotion. Motion No. 26A adds a Subclause (e) to Clause 6, the reporting section which would require the employer to report on:

We do not know how many visible minorities are sending in applications and being turned down, and so on. That is important in judging whether that firm is serious about improvement in its employment equity program. I am asking in Motion No. 26A that that sort of information be added to the report.

-implement employment equity by

They are going to have to say in their report what they have done to identify and eliminate each of the employer's practices that serve as barriers to people in the designated groups. Subclause (4b) reads that an employer shall implement employment equity by the following:

Mr. Speaker, with regard to these three motions, which have been submitted by the Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace- Lachine East (Mr. Allmand), all are amendments designed to improve the Bill to provide definitions. One would think that the Government Members would welcome these suggestions. Tragically, some of these have been proposed in committee. Although some of the committee members indicated there was value to some of these amendments, the committee was unwilling to give assent to these amendments at that time. The amendments we have suggested in the last three days and the amendments we are debating today are designed to improve the Bill. These three amendments can greatly improve the specifics of the Bill.
If government Members can boast that their strength is their inability to think for themselves, then surely the Tories can be called invincible. It is sad that no Government Members are prepared to stand up and explain why they oppose these amendments which are designed to improve the Bill. I might explain to those who might be listening that the reason the walls in this place is resounding is that there are so few Members here from the Government. In fact, saying there is a corporal's guard would be exaggerating. In any event, they vote the same way and are uninterested in examining the value of the amendments. There is no willingness to examine what is being offered.
The amendment would include not just those who are promoted but also those who are trained, transferred, demoted and terminated. This would obviously improve the Bill. However, it seems that the Government does not want to accept suggestions from anyone because it believes that it must stand by what it has written and that it must be accepted as perfect. To admit that there could be improvements may in some way minimize its omniscience. Everyone knows the Government is not omniscient and it need not pretend to be.
It is unfortunate that it is not prepared to listen and seriously consider these amendments. The Government claimed that it would be open to consultation and dialogue. However, there is no response to dialogue and there has been no consultation because most of these resolutions we have brought forward have been proffered by the groups that are affected. It does not matter that we have offered the opinions of COPOH, women's organizations and native people-the

April 15, 1986
Employment Equity
Government has made up its mind that it knows best. It is autocratic, it is paternalistic, and one might say that it is ruthless. It will not listen despite all of the highest claims that it would enter into a new era. There is a complete lack of response to the suggestions in these motions.
I want to use this occasion to say that these motions involve technical changes that would improve the Bill. Perhaps between now and the time we vote on these motions the Government might consider accepting some of them on the basis that it has had time for repentance and of its willingness to accede to the fact that these suggestions may improve and strengthen the Bill. I hope the Government will take some of the major clauses into account and attempt to rectify them. These motions involve technical improvements which, if not passed now, hopefully will appear in the guidelines. The Government is not impressing the handicapped, native people or anyone with its obturate and stubborn attitude.

Mr. Speaker, these amendments reflect need, logic, common sense and fairness. They have been suggested by the affected groups, and perhaps that explains why they will be rejected by the Government like the other constructive amendments which have been offered.
First, let us consider Motion No. 25A. It states:
That Bill C-62, be amended in Clause 6 by striking out line 39 at page 3 and
substituting the following therefor:
"moted, trained, transferred, demoted and terminated and the degree of".
I received a letter from a group representing minority employees in the Public Service. They told us that because of the ineffectual affirmative action program in the Government of this country and the Public Service, members of visible minority groups were being demoted, transferred and terminated-all of those things which are mentioned in the motion. The remedies which this Act should provide should extend beyond mere hiring, promotion and termination. Therefore, this amendment should be accepted by the Government because of its logic, fairness, common sense and need.
Let us consider Motion No. 26A. It states:
That Bill C-62, be amended in Clause 6 by adding immediately after line 41
at page 3 the following:
"(e) the number of individuals in designated groups who apply for specific
openings".
Let us assume that we have counted the number of minority groups in the employ of a particular employer and determined the distribution of the designated groups in the population but will only consider what happens to those already employed, of which there are likely to be few. What good is that exercise if we do not determine the hiring practices of the company?
Motion No. 27A addresses the fact that Clause 4 makes no specific provision for reporting the actions required of the employer to the Minister or to anyone else. It is curious that the amendment proffered by my colleague refers only to Clause 4. Let us turn back to Motion No. 24 moved by my
Party colleague which begins with the words: "containing information in". It goes on to read:
"accordance with the duties imposed on the employer under sections 4 and 5
and further in accordance with prescribed instructions indicating."
It goes on to say, "in the form and manner prescribed". This means that the company's plan with respect to process or goals would at least be reported to the Minister and at least be available through that means since the Government sneakily omitted reporting provisions from Sections 4 and 5.
The Parliamentary Secretary has the opportunity to reconsider his refusal to provide for reporting to employees by accepting Motion No. 24 and providing more details with respect to the treatment that might be accorded to the target groups by accepting these amendments. So I would ask him to reconsider and acknowledge these amendments as a useful contribution to strengthening this Bill. If he refuses to do so, that will be another concession by the Government that it is attempting to pull one grand joke on women, visible minorities, natives and the disabled.
My colleague mentioned earlier how few members of the Government were here to listen to this debate. Perhaps they ought to remember that half the population is made up of women and perhaps one person out of 20 in the population would benefit from employment equity provisions which apply to the disabled. They ought to know that the visible minority population of the country represents between 500,000 and 600,000 persons and that they are presently concentrated in certain areas.
If those Hon. Members think they are going to get away with this garbage with impunity, perhaps they had better reexamine their thinking. I believe there is a notion held by the Tories that women, the visible minorities, the disabled and native Canadians are not watching what is going on or are too stupid to understand. But they will not be fooled by this nonsense, this parade of fancy rhetoric, this voluntary employment equity program which offends every notion of how affirmative action programs ought to be designed. It is about time the Parliamentary Secretary and his Minister started to think about how to address the real needs of so many people in this country who are tired of having promises broken and equality delayed. Government Members delay equality and break promises when they sit here silent, listening to the debate but rejecting constructive changes, which these target groups to whom the Bill is supposed to be directed have asked for and, indeed, demanded.
In the end, two groups will suffer. Those Hon. Members opposite will suffer when those millions of individuals who should be benefiting from the Bill have lost hope. They will lose votes.

Mr. Speaker, there are a series of amendments here which are being proposed in order to improve the unimprovable. I think one has to ask oneself
April 1 5, 1986

whether it is really worth the effort given the fact that only part of the Bill which has any effect at all is the reporting requirement. As the amendments make clear, the reporting requirement is weak and could and should be improved. However, as 1 stated earlier during discussion of different elements of the Bill, the Bill as a whole is so ineffective that it is a pity it is called an employment equity bill. It might be better called a Bill on employment inequity or a Bill on delay to employment equity.
I would like to say that I was perhaps a bit more passionate a few moments ago when I was speaking about the secretive nature of the planned objectives and targets for employment equity. These things will not be shared with employees. However, I think an important opportunity is being lost by the House of Commons in this employment equity Bill. 1 know the Minister is extremely sensitive about the criticism she has received from members of the New Democratic Party with respect to the weaknesses in this particular Bill. I have been in politics long enough to recognize that not everything we hope for in a Bill will be there. Politics does require compromises and, and to some extent, some balance between the views of different groups, individuals and institutions in our society. Those things I am prepared to recognize, but when it comes to the Bill, it seems to speak almost entirely to the fears of business that it will somehow be made to do something it does not want to do. The Bill, therefore, purports to give some progress towards employment equity in order to cool down the various groups representing women, native Canadians, the handicapped and visible minorities, while in fact doing next to nothing. It seems to me that such is the nature of the compact which has been made with the business community. 1 regret to say that we are going to have to pass this Bill and it will be five years before anyone knows whether or not it works. There will be some reporting but it will not be very onerous. In the meantime, business can go on as if nothing has changed.
I do note that in certain areas of activity in the United States that country has gone further in terms of affirmative action than anything even envisaged in this Bill. I am speaking now in sorrow as much as in anger. The Government is not even prepared to make the reporting requirements adequately detailed with respect to the size of the companies which will mainly be affected so that they are to receive the kind of information which might be helpful as a starting point in measuring progress towards employment equity.
The Parliamentary Secretary has had in the past the reputation of being a man with progressive views. It is a pity that he finds himself in such regressive and reactionary company as is to be found within the Conservative caucus.
The Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) was known in her day as a red Tory. The red seems to be rapidly blending into blue, but it may very well be that she herself disagrees in a very fundamental way with a lot of things she has had to do in order to get this pale shadow, this thin thing, into the House of Commons as a Bill which purports to deal with employment equity. Perhaps she
Employment Equity
privately wishes she could have done a lot more. My message to the Parliamentary Secretary and to the Minister of Employment and Immigration is that there comes a time when one has to speak with one's conscience rather than simply being loyal to one's Party for reasons which are perhaps hard to defend when one is forced to do things one cannot live with or stomach.
Is the Minister of Employment and Immigration so negative and angry with the New Democratic Party because we are speaking truths about this particular Bill? We are telling her about the things which should be in the Bill. Has she had to reject these things because of pressure from reactionaries within her caucus and within the Cabinet? Was the Parliamentary Secretary so acid in his comments to me the other day because he also recognizes the weaknesses of this particular Bill? There is still time. I recognize that it will be a dramatic moment, but if members of the Government feel, as I do and as my Party does, that we have a commitment-perhaps those Hon. Members opposite share that commitment-to genuine affirmative action and employment equity, if there are still a few Tories who have that commitment, let them speak up now and vote against their Party when the amendments before us right now come to the fore. If that does not occur, I want the Parliamentary Secretary to take a message, not just to his Minister but to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) as well.
During the last election a lot of people were looking for change, including individuals in the different minority groups which are dealt with in this Bill, and they were prepared to change their political allegiance and support the Progressive Conservatives because they thought they were going to see a real change. I personally, and representatives of my Party, will go from coast to coast and will joke and mock the Progressive Conservatives over such things as the fact that the plans which were meant to be put forward for employment equity are so important that they are not going to be shared with the employees but are going to be kept secret. Any semblance of credibility developed by the Progessive Conservatives on this issue during their period of opposition is going to disappear utterly by the time we get to the next election. I speak the truth. That is the warning I want to give to the Parliamentary Secretary and to the Minister responsible for the Status of Women who is here with us in the House. She is perhaps only one of two Ministers in the House.
The credibility which his Party might have had is going down the drain. When people examine this legislation and see how weak it is, when they see from experience how little has changed as a consequence of it, then when the Conservatives say to native people, women, visible minorities and the handicapped: "See what a great job we are doing for you", they will be laughed at. No one likes to be laughed at, least of all members of the Government who came to power so proudly after the Liberal dynasty. They felt that they had ended that dynasty which had been around for such a long time. It was good that the Liberal dynasty was ended. What is bad is that

the present Government seems to be acting with exactly the same type of arrogance, insensitivity, inability to consult and understanding of the needs and aspirations of ordinary Canadians as the Government which it replaced. We saw how the electorate dealt with the previous Government as a result of the way it behaved toward ordinary Canadians. I tell the Parliamentary Secretary and the Ministers who are in the House now that the people of Canada will deal in exactly the same way with this Government as they did with the previous one if it continues to follow the same course.

Mr. Speaker, in concluding, perhaps I may say that today, in the province of Quebec, although the New Democratic Party failed to get any candidates elected, the fact that we tell the truth as reflected in the amendments we are proposing to this Bill on employment equity, did not go unnoticed by Quebecers, so much so that 26 per cent of the population has indicated that if an election were held today, it would vote for the New Democratic Party.

Clauses 4 and 5 refer to process, while Clause 6 refers to results which are to be reported. The stated intent of the legislation is that employers are required to report on results, not actions or programs. Clause 5 of the Bill clarifies that employers must have goals and timetables; but employers will develop their own process activities to achieve desired results.
With respect to Motion No. 25A, I do not see how it can be helpful. It is complicated. It would be difficult to see what information with respect to transfers would show. How would training be defined? Data collected on employees who were trained, transferred and/or demoted is not considered essential in monitoring the results of an employment equity plan. Training and transfers may be part of a plan to develop and broaden employee skills, but it does not actually reflect results of employment equity, where employment equity means more proportionate representation of designated groups. Any major changes which occur because of training, transfers or demotions will show up in a year-by-year comparison of data reported.
Motion No. 26A deals with "the number of individuals in designated groups who apply for specific openings". It is difficult to collect designated group data at the applicant stage. Proportionate representation in hirings will not be measured against the status of applicants but according to availability data, which may include more people than those who apply for a position.
With respect to Motion No. 27A, flexibility with respect to process is a basic philosophy of this Bill. The Bill's focus is on results of such acts, not the fact that employers report such acts. The employer's executive summary can provide information about measures taken in support of employment equity.

Mr. Speaker, earlier the Parliamentary Secretary said that the Government had an obligation to do everything to ensure equality and opportunity. Presumably he was making specific reference to the designated groups to which the Bill would apply. He also said that the proposed legislation was directed to the achievement of goals and oriented toward the achievement of results. This has been reiterated over and over again.
The fact is, as was pointed out by my colleague, that we would have an equally effective Bill if it were proposed that at nine o'clock every day of the week employers would get up and say: "I will not practise discrimination. I will treat the disabled, women, visible minorities and native people well today". In effect that is all Bill C-62 promises. We have come to the nub of the issue, the point at which the Government must decide whether or not it is serious. It must decide whether it is on the side of those employers which surveys indicate would reject affirmative action. By and large they would reject it, as the record would indicate, because they now have licence to practise a three-to-one bias against visible minorities. Of course the record in respect of native people, women and the disabled is clear. They would have us believe that voluntary affirmative action and voluntary employment equity is the answer. As was indicated earlier, Judge Abella was specifically assigned terms of reference requiring her to make a choice between voluntary affirmative action and mandatory affirmative action. It is perfectly clear that the judge carefully considered the alternatives. She made her decision on the basis of evidence which is unambiguous. The evidence from the United States was certainly clear that only mandatory affirmative action is worthy of consideration if one is serious about achieving equality in the workplace for the designated group. That is irrefutable.
The evidence is equally clear in Canada. The good judge looked at the evidence with respect to the employment of women in the Public Service and found that the result of nearly a decade of voluntary affirmative action has not been affirmative at all. There has been no significant progress in most areas. Women are still relegated to the clerical and lower administrative niches of the Public Service. Little progress has been made in achieving status, in significant numbers, at the management level.
Voluntary affirmative action has been attempted with respect to the disabled, and that has been equally a failure.
The federal Government has invoked voluntary affirmative action with respect to visible minorities, and I speak in particular of the program in Nova Scotia. The proportion of visible minorities employed in the federal Government during the period of voluntary affirmative action was 2.2 per cent of the workforce, whereas the percentage in the population was 4.4.
Mandatory affirmative action with specification of goals has worked undoubtedly, unquestionably, and unambiguously. One need only cite the non-voluntary affirmative action program with respect to the Francophone national linguistic group in the country. It was successful. I will assert here and now that if the French people of the country had been faced with a proposal for a voluntary equity program they would have rejected it, and their numbers would have caused their rejection to be taken seriously.
This proposed amendment would provide for penalties for the failure by an employer to proceed with the provisions of Clauses 4, 5 and 6. It presents the Government with an opportunity to ensure mandatory affirmative action. We do not want merely a reporting, on an annual basis, of the number of women, disabled, and visible minorities employed, but rather we want to have specified goals which must be achieved. That is mandatory affirmative action which was recommended by Judge Abella and which is unanimously demanded by all representatives of the designated groups.
The Government is now in a position to respond to those demands. It is at last in a position to be taken seriously because it will have manifestly taken a serious action in response to the cry for mandatory affirmative action which will respond to those in need rather than those who will be inconvenienced because they must correct the injustices of the past.

If this amendment is to be adopted, then the Bill would have some effect. Right now, the Bill does nothing for employment equity. It does provide a little bit of employment for clerks or other minor officials in some Department of the Government who will receive some reports from some employers and file them. It may provide some work for a post-graduate student who is doing a thesis 10 years from now and wants to look at some records. Apart from that, it will not provide work for the disabled, native people, visible minorities or women to the extent that they are now being mistreated and discriminated against in employment. That is a fact.
This subamendment would extend the penalty provision two ways: increasing it to $500,000 so that the big corporations would not laugh at the penalty; extend the penalty so that it applies to Clauses 4 and 5 of the Bill.
Those are the only clauses that, by themselves, have any real meaning.
Clause 4 begins very boldly by saying:
An employer shall, in consultation with such persons as have been designated by the employees to act as their representatives or, where a bargaining agent represents the employees, in consultation with the bargaining agent, implement employment equity by-
The way it is worded it says that the employer shall implement employment equity. It lays that on not just as good advice, not just as something that the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) wishes they would do or her Parliamentary Secretary wishes they would do, it says with the force of Parliament that the employer shall implement. He shall identify and eliminate the employment practices that result in employment barriers. He shall institute positive policies, making reasonable accommodation and ensure that persons in designated groups achieve a degree of representation that is at least proportionate to their representation in the workplace. The employer shall do these things.
Clause 5 goes on to say that the employer shall, in respect of each year, prepare a plan. He is going to make a plan that will set out the goals that the employer intends to achieve in implementing employment-what he is ordered to do in Clause 4-and the timetable.

With respect to the timetable, how many corrections is he going to make in his workforce next year and the year after so as to bring up a more just balance of the disadvantaged groups with which this Bill is supposedly concerned? The Minister has prated and preached about the court of public opinion. We know from experience in this country and in the United States that the court of public opinion cannot make most employers do those things the Minister claims this law makes them do. So the Minister's claim is not to be believed. Whether she can wake up in the morning and believe what she is saying is not the point. The point is that no one outside Parliament can believe it.
This is not only the opinion of members of the Opposition. This is the opinion which was expressed by the representatives of the very groups the Minister claims she wants to help. We are disturbed and disappointed by the Government's responses. We hope to be successful in persuading the Government to amend Bill C-62, which is presently before the House, to make it an effective tool for creating equality.

If employers do not voluntarily undertake affirmative action programs, and if their yearly reports on their workforce show no progress towards equality, nothing happens. Bill C-62 only requires reports. Reports are not enough.

of getting a job as a black person with the very same qualifications, said about the Bill, and I quote:

Member cut my remarks out once they have been printed so that he can use them in his speeches. It grew from 41.9 per cent in 1973 to 51.6 per cent in 1982. In 1967 the Royal Commission on the Status of Women looked at the problems which were creating economic difficulties for women in our society. These are two of the questions which were asked at that time: What was making older women poor in our society? What was the problem with part-time work? For the first time the women sat down together and drew up a list of the problems which they faced in an evolving 20th century society.
Following the report of the commission in 1967 we saw many issues undertaken, most of them voluntary. I am sorry to say that those voluntary issues which my Party put into place were not sufficient. That is why the Bill before us is necessary. It is necessary as mandatory legislation with enforcement principles.
In 1969 we saw the first of the revisions to the divorce laws which came about as a result of a great deal of economic suffering for families, and therefore pressures on women were created. There was an unfortunate series of family breakdowns of which we were not even aware. That is when the issue of the single-parent family first came to the fore.

itself in a voluntary way, then equal pay for work of equal value should be part of the mores of society, but it is not, and that is a key point.

In 1978, we took a good look at the Canada Pension Plan and put in equal splitting of pensions between spouses on divorce or annulment of a marriage. Members telling me that we did not do things that were sensitive and in the interests of women? Members look at those 114 legislative changes that were made and tell me that we did not bring in good, substantive legislative change.

Mr. Speaker, 1 would like to rise in support of the subamendment which was moved by the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Cassidy). In effect, that subamendment attaches a penalty to Clauses 4 and 5 of the Bill.

I would like to remind the House that we have had Bills like this. 1 recall the competition policy Bills brought into the House by the Liberal Government. Even Bill C-91, which was brought before the House the other day to provide for competition and control mergers, was, as were previous competition Bills, designed to give the impression that something was being done when in fact we were not really serious about doing anything. This Bill is of the same genre.
Clause 4 of the Bill reads as follows:
An employer shall, in consultation with such persons as have been designated by the employees to act as their representatives or, where a bargaining agent represents the employees, in consultation with the bargaining agent, implement employment equity by-
The clause goes on to indicate what they have to do. One must ask oneself, what if they do not do it? 1 have not been convinced that employers are really interested in creating a climate in the workplace which would eliminate the kinds of discriminatory practices which have existed. As a matter of fact, as reported by today's Toronto Star, Judge Rosalie Abella addressed the Canadian Club in Toronto.
The article reads in part as follows:
More women are working in Canada than ever before-but most are still "ghettoized" in the occupations they have been confined to since 1901-
The article goes on to say:
Sixty per cent of working women in Canada remain "occupationally segregated," receiving 60 per cent of men's wages, "an 11 per cent improvement over 70 years," Abella said.
The article goes on:
It's clear, that expectations about the role of women arc so deeply rooted "that without active and persistent intervention, the subtle barriers women experience will remain stalwartly erect."
Is the Tory Government a neophyte in this field? We realize it is inexperienced in governing. Perhaps Conservative Members are looking in the mirror and seeing their own reflections. As members of a business-oriented Party, they do not want to put some teeth in this Bill. We have enough legislation in Canada without any teeth. In this particular Bill, the only penalty provided is the filling out of forms as prescribed by Clause 6 of the Bill. If Hon. Members have not read it, I suggest they should, because Clause 6 creates more bureaucratic red tape for businesses and corporations. They have to fill out a form indicating how many employees they have and how many are working in certain sectors. If they do not file that form, they get a $50,000 fine.
The real meat of the Bill is employment equity, and that is where the penalty of $50,000 should apply. It should not apply for paper shuffling. All you guys are interested in is bureaucratic paper shuffling. That is what you are involved in. You are not involved in any meaningful changes. You are not interested in that at all.

Member for Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent) has obtained leave to move a motion for the adjournment of the House for the purpose of discussing a specific and important matter requiring urgent consideration, namely the attack of the United States against Libya

speechtext:
Thai this House do now adjourn.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the reason we are having this emergency debate tonight in the Canadian House of Commons is that within the past 24 hours there has been an attack by United States forces on Libya in many locations, in response to what the United States Government has described as a Libyan-sponsored act of terrorism in a West German nightclub not many days ago. According to President Reagan, the evidence for this specific Libyan link to what the whole world would describe as a deplorable act of terrorism is, to use President Reagan's words, "direct, precise and irrefutable". That is the contention of the President of the United States. If that turns out to be direct, precise and irrefutable, it is indeed a damning case made against the Government of Libya.
The Canadian interests in this tragic historic situation in the Middle East are twofold. First, there are upwards of 1,300 Canadians living in Libya and therefore we as a Parliament have a direct interest in and concern about the security of those Canadians. Second, like men and women in nations all over the world today, Canadians have to be assessing the implications of the response to the acts of terrorism which the United States has attributed to the Government of Libya; that is to say, we have to be concerned and we have to assess the response of one of the world's superpowers in this circumstance. 1 want to deal with both these questions, the Canadian situation specifically and the broader international implications of the situation in the Middle East today. First I make clear, and I am sure I speak for all Members of Parliament on this particular matter, that anyone living in a free and democratic society who believes in freedom and democracy has to abhor terrorist violence in all its forms. I take that as a given which all of us in Parliament share.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 29   EXTERNAL AFFAIRS U.S.-LYBIA CONFRONTATION-SAFETY OF CANADIAN CITIZENS
speechtext:
The use of violence against men, women and children to express a political will in a free society is completely and utterly abominal, and I am sure everyone in this Parliament agrees with that. The use of violence, I say immediately, in an unfree society, as the Catholic Church has recently noted, sometimes regrettably becomes a moral necessity. That is an entirely different circumstance. We are
talking about violence against innocent people in free societies as a political weapon.
1 have done some checking into the matter of violence in Europe over the past 12 months. Apart from the Middle East itself, almost all the violence in the past few years about which we have been concerned, to put it in those terms, has been violence that has taken place in European countries-Spain, Belgium, West Germany, Austria, Greece, Italy, Ireland and Sweden. All these countries in the past 12 months have had acts of violence within their borders. These are free, democratic, peace-loving societies. I could go outside these northern democratic nations and talk about violence elsewhere in the world, but I am restricting my comments and observations now to that part of the world alone to say that even in genuinely free societies where means are available to all citizens to bring about political change, this modern plague of terrorism has been demonstrating its evil force.
In a few moments I will come to the European reaction to the course of action taken by President Reagan in the present circumstances. However, before doing that, I want to pause and briefly consider the Canadian situation in this important matter. Unless the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Nielsen) who will be participating in the debate shortly has some different information to give us, the information which is most current in terms of news broadcasts is that no Canadians have been injured in any way. For that we as Canadians can be thankful, but there are some unanswered questions which have to be answered by the Government.
I want to say at the outset, and I do not say it lightly, that I think on a matter this serious, affecting Canadians as well as the international order and the principle of international law, the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Mulroney) ought to have been here to participate and to explain the Government's case. I regret that he is not participating in this debate.

There are a number of questions which I think ought to be answered and have not yet been answered by the Government of Canada. 1 want to list some of them, and 1 hope the Deputy Prime Minister will deal with them.
For example, has the Government or has it not spoken directly in the past 12 hours to Libyan authorities to ascertain whether or not the Canadians who are still in Libya and want to leave that country are able to do so without any hindrance whatsoever? It seems to me that the Government ought to have answered that question today, and it did not. Has the

April 15, 1986
Government provided aircraft and made it known to Canadians that they will facilitate their exit if they so desire?
I would like to know, as I asked yesterday and as the House Leader of the New Democratic Party specifically asked today, when the Prime Minister was informed of the specific nature of the plan of attack or approach that was to be taken by the United States. Did he know this before last Friday when he said in the House: "There is no immediate cause for undue concern for Canadians"? Again that question was not answered today in the House of Commons. We are not concerned here with quibbling about a small matter of history; it is a rather important matter. We now know, for example, that Margaret Thatcher knew about the middle of last week, and there is good reason to believe-and I will not put it any stronger than that-that the Prime Minister of Canada knew about the same time.? We attempted to obtain that information earlier today; we did not. 1 say to the Deputy Prime Minister that he has an obligation tonight when he speaks to come totally clean with Members of Parliament and the people of Canada about the degree of knowledge the Canadian Government had and when it obtained that knowledge. We want that information.
These are not matters in a particular order of importance. They are all important to us and to the people of Canada, in what the Deputy Prime Minister has described the ongoing discussions with the United States in the past week or so. We want to know on this side of the House, and virtually every European Government would like to know 1 suspect, with the exception of Margaret Thatcher in England, what proposals were made by the Government of Canada to President Reagan as alternatives to the use of violence. Did we have something to suggest concretely, and if we did, will the Government now tell the people of Canada what we suggested to President Reagan?
Beyond these important Canadian questions to which we would like answers, there is the broader question on which I would like to spend some time, namely, whether under the present circumstances in the Middle East the United States ought to have used its power in a military attack on a number of targets in Libya.
Is the death of an American soldier in a dance hail or a club of some kind in West Berlin-as horrendous and as horrible as it was, and it was an action to be deplored by us all-a cause for response such as that taken by the United States? Is it appropriate to use military forces and attack another nation's capital and kill-we do not know the numbers yet-a number of innocent victims as retribution for an earlier abominable act, assuming for a moment that the evidence is very clear that the Libyan Government itself is responsible for the murder that took place, and that is what it is, in West Germany? Surely that is a fundamental question.
As well, Margaret Thatcher, who has always supported President Reagan quite clearly in the past, has said that when you deal with violence and acts of terrorism, the response has
to be commensurate with the act itself. You have the violent death of a young American soldier on the one hand and you have this response. I am raising the question; whether that is appropriate. I want to raise some related questions about that.
As I mentioned a minute ago in listing the countries in western Europe, there has been great concern in the past 12 months among the peoples of western Europe with violence. They have lived with it much more than we have in this part of the world, not only in the past 12 months but in the past dozen years. They have had to live with a modern form of political terrorist violence in democratic society. One would have thought that under such circumstances the United States of America would have considered very seriously the views of their friends and allies in western Europe.
I have been on the phone today with people in West Germany and with people in Great Britain, Government and non-government sources, to get from them their response to what President Reagan has done in the present circumstances.
What do we know, Mr. Speaker? We know that one of the most respected foreign affairs ministers in the world-not simply in Europe, but the present foreign minister of West Germany, who does not belong to my Party, Hans Dietrich Genscher-was en route by air yesterday bringing a message, not simply from his Government but from the whole European Parliament. All the Governments in the European Parliament, with the exception of the Government of the United Kingdom, wanted to send a clear message to President Reagan late yesterday. That clear message was: "Don't use force. Don't take military action at this time". He was speaking at that time for his Government and, I repeat, for all the other governments in western Europe except that of the U.K.
We now know also that France and Spain not only opposed this action, but refused the granting of their airspace to the American aircraft en route to their attack in Libya. That is how strongly the Governments of Spain and France, which have had to deal with terrorism themselves, felt about this action by the United States. The Government of the Netherlands has publicly condemned the action; Prime Minister Craxi of Italy has publicly condemned the action by the United States. The West German Government, I was informed just before coming into the House tonight, described the American action as scarcely understandable.
I ask you, Mr. Speaker, to consider the response of all these countries which have had to live with terrorism and which are democratic societies, not namby-pamby or wishy-washy, but made up of serious men and women who want to maintain peace in their own society for their own members. They want to maintain international order and international law. They have said under these circumstances to the United States that a wise superpower knows when not to use its power. They have objected very clearly. Why have they objected very clearly? Why, Mr. Speaker?
One reason was given to me in a conversation with a former Chancellor of the Exchequer of Great Britain. He said that in
April 15, 1986

his understanding, and in that of most international law experts, the United States has violated international law. It is as simple and as clear as that, in his view. It is as important as that. It is a violation of international law; not according to some young person or some activist but, I repeat, according to a former Chancellor of the Exchequer of the U.K. who told me that that is a commonly held view in Europe. There is an objection to a democratic state like the United States, which ought to be upholding the principles of law, going against international law.
The second reason, for which they are opposed is that this kind of violence by the state-because that is what it is when you use military force-simply does not work. It has had a tendency, a history, of simply causing repetition, more violence.
I ask the Prime Minister through you, Mr. Speaker, to consider a man like Mr. Khadafy. We would like to see evidence in this case, but let us assume that the Libyans are guilty. We know they have been guilty before. It is quite possible they were. We know that Mr. Khadafy is quite an irrational man. We know that moderate states in the Middle East like Egypt have been wanting for a long time to put distance between themselves and Mr. Khadafy. We know that the Soviet Union for a long time has wanted to put distance between itself and Mr. Khadafy. When a superpower uses this kind of violence against a Government headed by this kind of man, how is he likely to respond? Is he likely to respond calmly, coolly and rationally? Is he likely to say "Oh, my goodness, I better not do any more violent things because they may hit us again"? Not at all. That is a profound misunderstanding in my view of modern terrorism. The more likely response from such a man is to accelerate his own violent propensities. If it does not happen this week, this month or a month from now, the likelihood is that we can see more acts of violence in the future by Mr. Khadafy, violence of the kind we have seen in the past. I suggest that this kind of response is not likely to be very effective at all. It is likely to produce just the opposite of what is intended.
The other concern 1 have relates to the Middle East, and I am going to come to the broader question with regard to the Middle East in a moment. Some years ago the courageous Egyptian Government worked out the Camp David Accord with the Israelis and the United States. The very courageous head of the Egyptian Government, Anwar Sadat, moved in a constructive way. Ever since then the Egyptian people have been under pressure in the Arab community to lend support, from time to time, to more violent regimes. The western world, including the United States, has caused all kinds of emotional tension and conflict among the Egyptian people, and others who will be emotionally drawn toward Mr. Khadafy. When one of their own is attacked, the immediate tendency is to move with their own, rather than against them.

Indeed, we have already heard about an attack, allegedly initiated by Libya in the early hours this morning in response to the attack made on that country. However, there is a stronger list, in terms of effectiveness of approaches which ought to have been pursued, and which our Government ought to be urging upon the Government of the United States.

It should partake in tough economic sanctions. I remind Members of Parliament that in 1980 we passed an Act of Parliament with reference to the Iranian crisis. It was a measure that had teeth, a measure of economic sanctions. It had punitive provisions for violation. We set an example, because in that instance there was a clearly perceived act of terrorism under way in the form of a hostage taking.
There is a variety of sanctions which can be taken. By way of example, there is no real movement to get rid of the apartheid regime in South Africa. Our Government has stated that it is prepared to act in terms of economic sanctions. With regard to acts of terrorism instead of using the state power with equal acts of terrorism, we should be using law and economic sanctions. That is the kind of thing which makes sense.

The world knows that certain state members of Interpol have been involved in state terrorism, so that is not effective. I suggest that we, with other like-minded states, perhaps the Europeans and the Americans, make a determined effort to coordinate anti-terrorist police investigations among ourselves, creating a special council of Ministers representing our

April 15, 1986
Governments which would have the responsibility of coping in a tough way with international violence, which Interpol has not been able to act upon. That is a practical proposal I would like to see tried.
I would like to conclude with the following observation. We as a nation must recognize the historical origin of terrorism in the Middle East-not to condone it. To recognize the human and sociological origin of crime is not to condone crime. However, if you do understand some of the background you can cope with it more adequately, and remove it in some cases. To understand modern political terrorism which comes out of the Middle East we must have other than a mad-dog view of human history. The truth is that most terrorist activities coming from Arab countries is directly related to the very sad post-war history of the Palestinians and their quest for a homeland. The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) in his recent statement made in the Middle East showed that there is one member of the Government who has some understanding of what is required historically.
